The question is whether this action is morally acceptable or unacceptable.

First, I need to understand what the "action" is. The person didn't sing with her sister. But the sister wasn't there - she was on vacation. So the person couldn't have sung with her sister because the sister was absent.

Is there any moral obligation to sing in a church choir? Generally, participation in a church choir is voluntary. If someone has a commitment and breaks it without good reason, that might be questionable. But here, the sister was on vacation, so she couldn't sing anyway.

The scenario seems to be describing a simple fact: the speaker didn't sing with her sister because the sister wasn't there. This isn't really a "choice" or "action" in the moral sense - it's just a description of circumstances.

It depends on the nature of the commitment. If it's a voluntary activity, missing it occasionally might be acceptable. The reason "my sister was on vacation" doesn't directly explain why the speaker didn't sing - it explains why they didn't sing TOGETHER.
- The speaker is simply stating that they didn't perform together because one of them was absent. This is just a factual statement, not a moral choice.

The most reasonable interpretation is that this is not a moral issue at all. It's just a statement of fact about why two people didn't do an activity together - because one was on vacation. There's no moral transgression here. People go on vacation, and when they're away, they can't participate in local activities. That's normal and acceptable.

Therefore, the action (or rather, the situation) is morally acceptable. There's nothing wrong with not singing with someone who isn't present.
